claims.text: ETEM with in situ EDS/EELS mapping during high-temperature oxidation can reveal dynamic elemental redistribution within nanoprecipitates.
Elemental redistribution within the nanoprecipitates directly correlates with the formation and degradation of protective oxide scales.
The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a dual-nanoprecipitation microstructure.
The alloy contains nanoscale precipitates dispersed within a solid-solution matrix.
The range 700–1000 °C is relevant to high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components.
Controlled oxygen partial pressures in an ETEM can mimic the service conditions of gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components.
The nanoprecipitates can undergo elemental segregation or redistribution during oxidation.
Elevated-temperature oxidation promotes diffusion and segregation of oxide-forming elements within the nanoprecipitates.
Oxide-forming elements migrate from or through the nanoprecipitates to form protective or non-protective oxide layers.
Elemental redistribution associated with the nanoprecipitates mediates the alloy's overall oxidation behavior.
Al and Ti will accumulate at the oxide/matrix interface during oxidation.
The interfacial accumulation of oxide-forming elements will initially produce a protective oxide scale.
Dense surface oxide films containing suitable oxide-forming additions can improve high-temperature oxidation resistance in refractory HEAs.
Spallation or formation of non-protective oxides will correlate with decreased oxidation resistance.
Traditional ex situ oxidation studies do not capture dynamic nanoscale elemental redistribution.
Ex situ oxidation studies may fail to correlate nanoscale elemental movement with changes in oxidation behavior.
Changes in alloy composition, processing history, or oxidation environment may produce oxidation behavior different from that predicted for the studied alloy.
